value.overview: The Wood Duck (Aix sponsa) is a colorful, medium-sized perching duck associated with wooded freshwater habitats. It has a compact body, broad tail, and strong claws that help it perch in trees. Adult males are especially striking, with a glossy green and purple head, white facial markings, a red eye, and a chestnut breast. Females are gray-brown with a noticeable white eye-ring. The species is native mainly to North America.
value.classification: The Wood Duck belongs to the order Anseriformes and the family Anatidae, which includes ducks, geese, and swans. Its scientific name is Aix sponsa.
value.identification: The male has an iridescent green-and-purple crested head, white lines around the face, a red eye, a reddish bill, a chestnut breast, and patterned flanks. The female is mostly gray-brown, with a rounded crest, a white eye-ring, and a pale throat. Both sexes have a long, squared tail and a relatively large head. In flight, dark upperparts contrast with a pale belly and light wing markings. Its habit of resting on branches can also be distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: Wood Ducks breed across much of eastern and central North America, along the Pacific coast, and in parts of southern Canada and western Mexico. They favor wooded swamps, bottomland forests, freshwater marshes, ponds, beaver wetlands, and slow-moving streams with dense shoreline vegetation and nearby tree cavities. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular resident or breeding duck. It has been recorded there as a very uncommon visitor or vagrant, mainly at suitable freshwater wetlands, ponds, and forest-edged waterways; sightings are unusual and localized.
value.migrationStatus: The Wood Duck is partly migratory. Northern birds move south in autumn, while many birds in the southern part of the range remain year-round. Costa Rica lies well south of the principal regular range, so occurrences there are best treated as rare, irregular records rather than a predictable migration passage or wintering population.
value.breeding: Wood Ducks nest in natural tree cavities, often near or above water, and readily use nest boxes. The female lines the cavity with down and usually lays 6–16 creamy white to tan eggs. Incubation lasts about 28–37 days. Ducklings leave the cavity soon after hatching by climbing or jumping to the ground and following the female to water. Most pairs raise one brood, although two broods can occur, especially in southern parts of the range. There is no reliable evidence of regular breeding in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of plant material, including seeds, acorns, fruits, aquatic vegetation, and agricultural grains. Wood Ducks also eat insects, beetles, caterpillars, flies, snails, isopods, and other small invertebrates, with animal foods often more important during breeding. They feed by dabbling in shallow water, picking food from vegetation or the surface, and walking on land beneath trees to gather fallen nuts and fruit.
value.behavior: Wood Ducks are agile fliers and usually remain close to cover rather than spending long periods on open water. They perch on branches and logs, swim quietly through vegetation, and forage in shallow water. Pairs form during the winter and display with head movements, raised wings, and mutual preening. Females sometimes lay eggs in the nests of other Wood Ducks. After hatching, ducklings leave the cavity together, while the female calls them toward nearby water.

conservation.populationTrend: The population is considered stable to increasing overall, with substantial recovery after severe declines caused by overhunting and loss of nesting habitat in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
